newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan leader pledges to honour any IMF accord.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan leader pledges to honour any IMF accord.

text.p: Former Pakistani prime minister Nawaz Sharif promised on Thursday to uphold any IMF deal reached by the caretaker government if he wins elections on February 3.

Sharif, leader of the Pakistan Muslim League which was in power from 1990 to 1993, told a news conference that any government must abide by commitments made to the International Monetary Fund or World Bank by its predecessors.

"I think we are duty-bound to honour any such commitments Pakistan makes to the IMF, World Bank or any other country," he said. "It is not any particular government that is signing, it is the country, Pakistan, which is signing."
The IMF was known to have been concerned about whether accords negotiated with the caretaker government led by Meraj Khalid would be honoured by an incoming elected government.

President Farooq Leghari, who sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule, has vowed to ensure that the next government would implement agreements signed with multilateral lending agencies.

Bhutto attacked Leghari on Wednesday over the issue, saying in a strongly worded letter to him that signing an agreement with the IMF now would be "making a mockery of the entire democratic process and the sovereignty of parliament itself".
She said the caretaker government had no legal right to enter into any long-term agreement with the IMF.

"If the national interest so demands that an agreement should be signed, then the two largest parties and their leaders must not only be taken into confidence about the conditionalities, but also agree to them," she wrote.

"The people of Pakistan are not prepared to have the (presidency) with its unelected and unelectable cronies rubber stamp four years of their destiny behind closed doors, in secrecy which will mortgage their future," Bhutto wrote.

Khalid's adviser on finance and economic affairs, Shahid Javed Burki, is due in Washington for talks with the IMF and World Bank next week. He wants to revive a stalled $600 million IMF standby loan and initiate talks on a longer-term IMF lending programme known as an enhanced structural adjustment facility.
Burki, who is on a three-month leave from the World Bank, is expected to ask the bank for a $200 million loan for balance of payments support and a loan to support financial sector reform.
Sharif said Pakistan needed a strong, stable government to tackle its problems, particularly the economy and law and order.

He promised that if he came to power he would convert an anti-corruption ordinance drafted by the caretaker government into law and strengthen an accountability commission set up to probe corruption complaints against politicians and bureaucrats.
